items.title: US Market: Fed’s Hammack says jobs data gives time to assess rate path
items.summary: Federal Reserve officials have signalled they have time to assess incoming economic data before making further changes to interest rates. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said Septembers weak employment report was broadly consistent with recent labour-market trends. With hiring slowing but remaining stable and inflation pressures persistent, policymakers are weighing employment and price stability before the next rate decision.

items.title: Gold inches up as October Fed rate hike prospects fade
items.summary: During early Monday trading in Asia, gold prices surged due to lackluster US job growth figures. This disappointing employment data notably diminished the Federal Reserve's likelihood of raising interest rates in October, prompting investors to pivot towards safe-haven assets. Spot gold climbed to $4,153.32 per ounce, while silver and platinum also experienced price increases as market reactions unfolded. Economic trends are steering investment behaviors in precious metals significantly.

items.title: Wall Street week ahead: Fed minutes, unemployment data, consumer sentiment update
items.summary: Wall Street has a busy week ahead with a mix of economic updates and details about the Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates at its last meeting. The updates include fresh data on the health of the services sector, unemployment and consumer sentiment. Those reports can help give investors and economists more insight into how businesses and households are adapting to persistently high inflation. The minutes from the Fed’s last meeting will also give Wall Street more details about the central bank’s decision-making process for interest rate policy.

items.title: What a hiring slowdown signals about the state of the U.S. economy
items.summary: U.S. hiring slowed in September as employers added just 29,000 jobs. The disappointing jobs report has wide-reaching implications for consumer prices and interest rates, and it comes a month before Americans head to the polls for midterm elections. Amna Nawaz discussed more with Beth Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland.
